content: The epidermis is the outermost layer of the skin. It serves as a waterproof, protective barrier that covers the surface of the body. Structurally, it is composed of stratified squamous epithelium supported by an underlying basal lamina. The epidermis lacks blood vessels and instead receives nourishment through diffusion from the dermis. The primary cell types found in the epidermis include keratinocytes, melanocytes, Langerhans cells, and Merkel cells. The epidermis is organized into several layers. New cells are generated through mitosis in the innermost layers. These cells gradually migrate upward through the strata, undergoing differentiation and becoming filled with keratin. As they progress, their shape and composition change. Eventually, they reach the outermost layer, known as the stratum corneum, where they are shed or desquamated. This process, called keratinization, occurs over the course of several weeks. The outermost layer of the epidermis consists of 25 to 30 layers of dead cells. The epidermis is further divided into five distinct sublayers, listed from superficial to deep: Stratum corneum Stratum lucidum Stratum granulosum Stratum spinosum Stratum germinativum (also referred to as the stratum basale) To aid in memorizing these layers, mnemonics are often used. For example: From superficial to deep: Corn Lovers Grow Several Bales. From deep to superficial: Before Signing, Get Legal Counsel. Additional visual aids include: A section of the epidermis.
